title: User-Aware Active Knowledge Acquisition for Emotional Support Dialogue
claim: Generic supportive replies mismatch implicit user needs; actively acquiring user-aware knowledge and selecting responses disambiguates needs and improves coverage and alignment.
layout: 3 panels left-to-right, dashed dividers, chat bubbles with color-coded blue/green backgrounds
description: A three-panel motivation figure separated by dashed vertical lines. Panel (a) shows a user saying 'I want empathy' and a chat. In a blue block, a generic assistant gives a templated reply and gets 'Just don't lecture me' pushback, marked in red. A green block below shows an assistant with retrieved EQ knowledge asking a clarifying question, and the user discloses their real feeling. Panel (b) has two stacked boxes. In the blue one, the system stays close to existing knowledge: a knowledge-base scatter with clustered points feeds a Knowledge/LLM Distribution column. In the green one, the assistant asks an informative question and the scatter gains new points, giving better coverage. Panel (c) shows two users with the same sad message but different needs (empathy vs. objective analysis). An EQ knowledge anchor box sits at the top, and smiley and frowny faces show the different outcomes. Red and green text carries the good/bad contrast.
caption: Motivation for User-Aware Active Knowledge Acquisition in emotional support dialogue. (a) EQ knowledge may help clarify a user’s needs, which are often implicit; generic supportive replies can mismatch the need and trigger pushback. (b) If interaction stays close to existing knowledge, the system collects redundant signals; actively selecting responses yields better coverage. (c) The same surface emotion may reflect different user preferences, requiring user-aware knowledge and response selection to achieve alignment.
abstract: Emotional support plays an important role in dialogue systems, and its success depends on adapting to a user's evolving and implicit needs across multi-turn interactions while leveraging the strong reasoning capacity of large language models. However, since signals about user needs are often weak, indirect, and can only be disambiguated through multi-turn interaction, existing emotional support methods often struggle to acquire and generalize relevant conversational knowledge efficiently. To bridge this gap, we introduce User-Aware Active Knowledge Acquisition (UKA), a gradient-free active dialogue learning framework that explicitly represents uncertainty about user needs and incorporates active learning into both knowledge acquisition and response selection.We propose a Theory-of-Mind uncertainty estimation mechanism that allows the model to prioritize responses, thereby eliciting more informative user feedback. UKA is capable of efficiently exploring user-aligned conversational knowledge during training while maintaining robustness at test time. Experiments across multiple dialogue benchmarks and model architectures demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms strong baselines in dialogue quality and user alignment.
